assigned: Lirael passes the folded note to her contact at the market stall.
authorRaw:
The spice merchant’s stall was a riot of scent—cinnamon bark curled like shards of sunset against the woven reed mats, saffron threads glowing like embers in the dusk, and peppercorns rattling like dry bones in a wooden bowl. The air clung to the back of my throat, thick as the crowd pressing forward. My fingers tightened around the folded note in my pocket, the wax seal cracked enough to catch the light if I dared.

I stepped past a woman whose sleeves were striped with dye the color of deep tidewater, her silver bracelets chiming like the rising tide. The stall’s owner—a broad-shouldered man with a face like sun-cracked oak—was already reaching for a jar of star anise when the commotion started three stalls over. A shout, a scuffle, the sharp cry of a child cut off by the press of bodies. The crowd surged away from the noise, and for one breath, the path to the note’s recipient opened.

There she stood, her dark braid threaded with shell beads I recognized from last quarter’s accounting ledger. She was scanning the crowd, her posture that of someone used to being overlooked until she wasn’t. My pulse stuttered—less the fear of discovery, more the instinct to step forward before I’d decided to.

The note burned against my palm.

A hand clamped my shoulder—too heavy, too deliberate to be accidental. I turned to find a man whose smirk suggested he’d been born knowing exactly where to plant himself in a crowd. His hair was the color of old parchment, his eyes the pale, unsettling gray of winter clouds. “You look like you’re carrying a secret,” he said, voice low and smooth as the oil merchants used to polish their seals. “Or a debt.”

I forced my mouth into something resembling a smile, the gold-capped tooth catching the light. “Just the weight of the day,” I said, letting the note slip a fraction further into my pocket. The metal of the earring at my ear was warm against the cool evening air.

He leaned closer, close enough that I caught the scent of salt and something faintly metallic—like the sea after a storm. “A note’s a heavy thing to carry for a debt that small.” His gaze flicked to my hand, hovering just above the pocket. “Unless it isn’t yours to pay.”

The note wasn’t his to question. It wasn’t mine to explain.

Before I could answer, the spice merchant’s voice cut through the noise, sharp with authority. “Enough. No more browsing—sell or move on.” The crowd shifted again, and the stall owner’s eyes met mine, flicking to the pocket where the note hid. The silence between us wasn’t quiet; it was a held breath.

The man beside me didn’t step away. He stayed close, too close, his presence a shadow I couldn’t shake. The note’s edges bit into my fingers. I could feel the world narrowing, the space between us shrinking.

I had to move. I had to act.

And then—

A bag of crushed coriander split open at my feet, spilling its golden dust across the reed mats like a deliberate rupture. The merchant’s curse was lost in the sudden gasp of the crowd. The man beside me shifted, distracted for the first time since he’d found me.

I took my chance.

The note passed from my hand to hers before I could second-guess it. A whisper of contact, a breath of shared air. Her fingers closed around it, warm and certain.

The stall owner’s voice rose again, sharp with command. “Clean it up. Now.”

I didn’t wait to see if she opened it. Didn’t linger to watch her reaction.

I walked away, the weight of the note gone but the tension coiled tight in my chest. The spice merchant’s shout followed me, but the words blurred into the hum of the market, the scent of crushed coriander clinging to my boots.

The deck was still warm in my hand.
prose: The spice merchant’s stall sat at the heart of the market, its wares spilling over every surface. Cinnamon bark lay in dark curls, star anise caught the dim light, and dried violet petals released a scent that lingered in the air. I wove between bodies, my fingers brushing the folded note in my pocket until the paper’s edges bit into my palm. Ahead, the stall’s proprietor, Arwen, swayed behind the counter, her rings catching the firelight as she sorted a tray of oranges whose scent mixed honey with something older. She hadn’t noticed me yet. Good. I exhaled through my nose, the scent of crushed clove thick in the air. The note pressed against my thigh. It had to reach her. It had to mean something. Then the crowd shifted. A man shouldered past me, his elbow jabbing my ribs hard enough to knock the breath from my lungs. I hissed, stumbling into a woman carrying a basket of pomegranates. The fruit toppled, bursting against the cobbles in a wet explosion of red and white seeds. The woman shrieked, but my attention was already snagged by the way the stranger’s coat flared behind him—dark wool, expensive, the kind that didn’t belong in a spice market. It wasn’t just the coat. The man moved through the space between the stalls, the air giving way around him. And then he turned, and I saw his face. Julian. His left foot scuffed once against the cobbles before he stopped, and something in my chest lurched, leaving a gap. I should have looked away. I should have turned and walked the other way. But the note in my pocket suddenly felt heavier, the weight of it drawing me toward him. He tilted his head, just slightly, the corner of his mouth quirking. Not quite a smile. Not quite a dare. But enough. Arwen’s voice cut through the noise.“You there. You’re blocking my view.”She snapped her fingers at me, sharp.“Move.”I didn’t. Julian’s smile deepened, just for me, and I knew then—he could see it. The way my collar shifted against the skin of my neck. The way my fingers trembled against the note. He could see the choice I hadn’t made yet, and he was waiting.“You’re in my way,” Arwen snarled, her rings flashing as she gestured me aside. I ignored her. Julian stepped closer, the scent of salt and something wild reaching me.“You’ve been avoiding my calls,” he murmured, his voice low enough that Arwen wouldn’t hear.“Or have you just been waiting for the right moment to drop that?”His chin tilted toward my pocket. The note wasn’t just a message anymore. It was a weapon. Arwen’s voice rose again, shrill.“I said—”I pulled the note from my pocket, my thumb brushing the wax seal. His breath hit the space between us, carrying the faint bite of cardamom.“You don’t know what you’re holding,” he said, quiet.“But you’re about to find out.”The spice market fell silent. I met his gaze, the weight of the note drawing me forward.“Then tell me.”His heel lifted, then settled flat again.“Not here.”Arwen lunged, her hand clamping around my wrist.“Enough games. I don’t pay you to stand there looking pretty.”I yanked free, my pulse roaring in my ears. Julian’s fingers brushed the back of my hand as he stepped between us, shielding me from her glare. His touch was light. Intentional.“She’s with me,” he said, voice even. Arwen’s eyes flicked to me, then back to him. Her lips parted, but whatever she meant to say died on her tongue. His thumb pressed once against the inside of his own wrist.“We need to talk.”The note trembled in my grip. I nodded. The market moved around us. But in that moment, there was only him. Only the choice. Only the way his fingers curled around my wrist—firm, possessive. I swallowed hard.“Then talk,” I said.I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…
